custom.label: (no preset -- use the fields below)
custom.summary: Nothing is filled in for you; set the fields yourself. Pick any other preset to reproduce a published video exactly.

master.label: domesim-master-presentation.mp4
master.summary: THE BIG ONE. Every tool, the whole construction masterclass, the frankendome, the priced starter home and the factory case, with 13 math screens deriving every figure on camera. About 45 minutes; allow a few hours to render.

world.label: every-dome-in-the-world.mp4
world.summary: All twelve Dome Creator presets, each rebuilt live from the simulator's own modules and shown at true relative scale, with math screens for frequency, framing, price and efficiency.

world_chatgpt.label: ten-dome-builds-master-20260829-135242-chatgpt.mp4
world_chatgpt.summary: The accountable master cut: ten real Dome Creator presets with Dome Forge and Assembly Line context, a per-build material breakdown, a construction-event labor breakdown, and a modeled direct-sale price for each.

series.label: the-vance-network-mini-series.mp4
series.summary: All six episodes of the dome micro-drama, back to back: six cold hooks, six cliffhangers, one arc, and a finale that leaves a thread open. Rendered 1080x1920.

drama.label: ep-dome-001-high-council.mp4
drama.summary: EP_DOME_001: a 60-second vertical micro-drama in the dome. Four beats, five archetypes, and a camera the script directs. Rendered 1080x1920, because the framing is computed for 9:16.

wedge.label: eight-cuts-to-a-house.mp4
wedge.summary: Building the dome straight from the tree: raw 45-degree log sectors as members, bark out and pith in, forty pinwheel frames with every end square, and gasketed seams instead of shared struts. Ten math screens derive the tree's board feet, the honest 2x4 packing, the kerf, the joint and the 22-foot dome two trees size.

scratch.label: dome-from-scratch-geometry-to-pixels.mp4
scratch.summary: From nothing to a lit pixel: the twelve points phi places, the divide that makes the shape geodesic, the two strut lengths that fall out, and then the whole rendering chain -- tubes, normals, the vertex buffer, the camera matrices, the divide by w, the depth buffer, culling and the lighting sum. 18 math screens derive every figure on camera.

build.label: dome-construction-masterclass.mp4
build.summary: The 46-chapter construction lesson: geometry, cut lists, jigs, raising, skinning, and the mistakes that stop domes going up.

cuts.label: hubless-compound-cut.mp4
cuts.summary: The single hardest operation in a hubless dome: the compound cut, on both machines, with the jig between them.

hex.label: hex-dome-masterclass.mp4
hex.summary: Hexagonal domes: one strut length, twelve pentagons, and what raising the frequency costs.

zome.label: zome-construction-masterclass.mp4
zome.summary: Zomes: flat parallelogram panels, one strut length, and a true point on top.

line.label: assembly-line-energy-masterclass.mp4
line.summary: What building one dome costs the two people who build it, limb by limb.

franken.label: frankendome-build-v2.mp4
franken.summary: The mixed-stock dome: folded brackets, slack, settling, and what it actually cost.

look.label: dome-house-lookbook.mp4
look.summary: Two furnished domes, a cast of eight, hair built as strands, a wardrobe lofted from the body, and the composer refusing a fitting pod the shell has come down on.

hype6.label: frankendome-montage-v6.mp4
hype6.summary: The Frankendome montage, version six: themed shells, the four product lines, a faster cadence and a beat under it.

kick2.label: dome-kickstarter-v2.mp4
kick2.summary: The campaign film: the brim, the pony wall, running cost, radiative cooling paint and the ten points.

look_stills.label: dome house lookbook -- contact-sheet stills
look_stills.summary: One still from each of the lookbook's eleven chapters, with no narration and no video encode. The fast way to check the cast, the wardrobe and the composer shots before rendering the film.

master_stills.label: master presentation -- contact-sheet stills
master_stills.summary: Renders one still every two minutes through the master presentation, with no narration and no video encode. The fastest way to see what the film looks like without waiting hours for it.

scratch_stills.label: from scratch -- one still per chapter
scratch_stills.summary: A still from roughly each chapter of the from-scratch explainer, with no narration and no video encode. The quick way to check every diagram in the film without waiting for a full render.

world_stills.label: every dome in the world -- stills
world_stills.summary: A still from each chapter of the twelve-design film. Quick, and it shows every preset dome without a full render.

why.label: why-wedges-no-sawmill.mp4
why.summary: The combined wedge film: the frankendome and V brackets it grew out of, the mechanism chapters borrowed whole from `wedge`, and then the case -- two timed cutting sessions cross-checked against a geometric prediction, a wedge valued two independent ways, the store-bought overheads nobody counts, and a structural claim given as a crossover diameter rather than a verdict. 39 chapters, 16 math screens, about 21 minutes.

voice_audition.label: audition the house narration voice
voice_audition.summary: Generates a short MP3 in the house voice so you can hear it before committing to a multi-hour render.

render_all.label: rebuild every published video
render_all.summary: Renders every deliverable in this repository, one at a time, skipping any that already exist. This is a very long job -- many hours -- and it is the one that reproduces the whole published set from a fresh clone.

all_domes.label: all-domes-every-permutation.mp4
all_domes.summary: ALL DOMES. Every Dome Creator preset drawn by the Creator's own renderer -- wood grain, glass, mirror tiles, real foundations and the equipment inside -- one dome assembled step by step in the tool's own construction order, then a sweep of every menu the customizer has, eight domes drawn at random, and the arithmetic of how many buildings that adds up to.

all_domes_stills.label: all domes -- one still per chapter
all_domes_stills.summary: A still from each chapter of the Dome Creator showcase, with no narration and no video encode. The quick way to check every dome, sweep and cut-away before committing to the full render.

dome_park.label: dome-park-bring-your-own-home.mp4
dome_park.summary: DOME PARK. The Kickstarter cut: an RV park for houses. A host builds a serviced pad, a dome owner brings the home and plugs in. Every pad and dome is drawn by the Dome Creator's own renderer, every figure comes from the park model -- including the ones that argue against the idea, which are on camera with the rest.

dome_park_stills.label: dome park -- one still per chapter
dome_park_stills.summary: A still from each chapter of the dome park pitch, with no narration and no video encode. The quick way to check every pad, landing, sweep and worksheet before committing to the full render.

ep-dome-001-high-council.mp4.note: The first micro-drama out of the narrative module: a 60-second vertical episode staged inside the dome, with the blocking, the proximity rings, the rig actions and every camera move computed by the drama director from a script JSON. Rendered 1080x1920 -- the 9:16 framing is the point, and a landscape render would discard it.

dome-house-lookbook.mp4.note: The interiors film: two furnished domes, a cast of eight built out of the same skeleton the lifting lesson uses, hair modelled as strands, a wardrobe lofted from the body's own cross-section, and the composer refusing a fitting pod because the shell has come down to meet it.

eight-cuts-to-a-house.mp4.note: The dome built straight from the tree: raw log sectors as structural members, forty independent pinwheel frames with no mitres anywhere, and gasketed seams instead of shared struts. Its math screens compute the trunk's board feet, pack 2x4s into the same sections honestly, cost the kerf, measure the joint and size the dome from the strut length the tree gives.

dome-from-scratch-geometry-to-pixels.mp4.note: From scratch, for somebody who has never written code: every calculation between one irrational number and a lit pixel. The shape (phi, subdivision, projection, two chord factors, a cut list) and then the picture (tubes, normals, the vertex buffer, the camera, the view and projection matrices, the divide by w, the viewport, the depth buffer, culling and the lighting sum), with 18 math screens deriving every figure on camera.

domesim-master-presentation.mp4.note: The master presentation: the toolchain tour, the whole construction masterclass, the frankendome, the priced starter home and the factory case -- with math screens that derive every figure on camera. Its segments (whoami, the party sting) are composed inside the lesson module, so this render must not compose them again.

every-dome-in-the-world.mp4.note: All twelve Dome Creator presets, each rebuilt live from the simulator's own modules and rendered at true relative scale, with math screens for the frequency ladder, hub versus hubless, price per square foot, envelope efficiency and scale.

ten-dome-builds-master-20260829-135242-c.note: A unique ChatGPT master cut: ten real Dome Creator presets, Dome Forge and Assembly Line context, plus a per-build material breakdown, construction-event labor breakdown and modeled direct-sale price.

why-wedges-no-sawmill.mp4.note: The combined cut. Where the method came from (the frankendome and its V brackets), what it is (borrowing the mechanism chapters and three math screens from `wedge` so the two films cannot disagree), and what it is worth -- from two timed cutting sessions that agree with a geometric prediction to 12%, a wedge valued two independent ways that land 1% apart, the store-bought overheads nobody counts, and a structural claim stated as a crossover diameter rather than a verdict.

two-trees-all-at-once.mp4.note: Registered by the project agent repair step: the harvest lesson was in the registry without a deliverable entry.

the-20-dollar-pine.mp4.note: Registered by the project agent repair step: the pine_value lesson was in the registry without a deliverable entry.

why-build-this-way.mp4.note: Registered by the project agent repair step: the why_build lesson was in the registry without a deliverable entry.

all-domes-every-permutation.mp4.note: The Dome Creator's whole catalogue drawn by the Creator's own renderer -- grain, glass, mirrors, foundations and the fit-out inside -- one dome built step by step in the tool's own construction order, then every menu swept one setting at a time, eight random draws, and the permutation count.

pvtwo-masterclass.mp4.note: Generated by the project agent film recipe: The Twenty Dollar Pine, Part Two.

dome-park-bring-your-own-home.mp4.note: The Kickstarter cut. An RV park for domes: what a pad is, built one step at a time; what it costs a host and what it returns; the measured hinge -- a dome's foundation is 8% to 63% of its build cost and on a pad the tenant never buys it; four ways to have a roof priced on one basis, and the month at which bringing your own home starts winning; one hardware set across three sizes; and a shell that comes off so the R-value can keep going up for as long as you own the house.

dome.label: 2V dome frame
dome.blurb: The geodesic frame itself, built from the project's real 2V geometry: 65 struts in exactly two lengths, 40 triangles, 26 hubs. Everything else is positioned against it.

shell_layers.label: Shell build-up
shell_layers.blurb: The wall as it really goes together, one layer at a time: insulation, sheetrock, sheathing, wrap, shingles, then the outer shell. Drive 'Layers shown' up across a shot to build the wall on camera.

solar_band.label: Solar array
solar_band.blurb: Photovoltaic panels laid on the actual dome triangles that face near enough to the sun. It picks the faces by angle, so the array is always a real, buildable set of panels.

hatch.label: Deck hatch
hatch.blurb: A watertight hatch with a raised curb, a hinged door and a locking wheel. 'Open' swings it.

plenum.label: Perimeter plenum
plenum.blurb: The ring duct around the base with louvred grilles: the air path that lets one blower hold a whole dome at negative pressure.

blower.label: Blower + hose
blower.blurb: The leaf blower on the ring, its nozzle, and the hose inlet on the far side. Turn 'Vacuum can' on for the suction story.

airflow.label: Moving air
airflow.blurb: The air itself, drawn as moving particles: room air sinking to the grilles, racing around the ring, and jetting outside. Switch 'Direction' to run the same loop backwards as a shop vacuum.

utility_column.label: Utility column
utility_column.blurb: The floor-to-crown column carrying water and power, with a lifting ring at the top. This is the answer to 'you can't put cabinets against a curved wall'.

interior_fixtures.label: Fixture blocks
interior_fixtures.blurb: Quick massing blocks for a kitchen, a bed and a bathroom, to show a floor plan working without modelling every appliance.

comparison_pair.label: Box vs dome
comparison_pair.blurb: A rectangular building and a dome side by side, both drawn from real dimensions you set, for an honest size comparison.

triangle_vs_square.label: Racking test
triangle_vs_square.blurb: The rigidity demonstration: push a plain square frame and it leans over; a triangle, or a square with one diagonal, does not.

door.label: Entry door
door.blurb: A framed door standing in the dome's lower band, with jambs, a header, a threshold and a handle. 'Open' swings the leaf.

window_band.label: Windows
window_band.blurb: Glazes the dome's own triangles in a band around the shell, so the windows are real panels of the structure rather than holes cut in it.

skylight.label: Skylight
skylight.blurb: Glazing over the crown triangles with a raised curb around the ring, for daylight straight down the middle.

wood_stove.label: Wood stove
wood_stove.blurb: A stove on a hearth pad with a flue running up to the crown. Turn the fire up and the firebox glows and heat rises.

water_tank.label: Water tank
water_tank.blurb: A cistern with hoop ribs, a tap and a visible water line. Animate 'How full' to fill or drain it on camera.

rain_catch.label: Rain catchment
rain_catch.blurb: A gutter ring around the base with a downspout. A dome is one continuous catchment surface, and this shows the water running down it into the ring.

battery_rack.label: Batteries + inverter
battery_rack.blurb: The off-grid power wall: a rack of cells with charge lights and an inverter cabinet beside it.

mini_split.label: Heat pump
mini_split.blurb: A ductless heat pump: the indoor head mounted on the shell and the condenser outside, joined by its line set. 'Air output' streams conditioned air off the head.

loft.label: Loft deck
loft.blurb: A mezzanine floor with a guard rail and a ladder. A dome's upper volume only counts as living space if you can stand on some of it.

deck.label: Outside deck
deck.blurb: An exterior deck with a rail and steps, sitting outside the door.

kitchen_run.label: Kitchen
kitchen_run.blurb: A counter run with a sink and tap, a range with burners, and a refrigerator. 'How much is there' brings them in one at a time.

furniture.label: Living set
furniture.blurb: A table with chairs around it and a sofa facing the middle -- enough furniture to read the room as somewhere people live.

wheelchair.label: Wheelchair + rider
wheelchair.blurb: A person in a manual wheelchair that follows one continuous route: up the entry ramp, in through the door, a full turn in place, and a tour of the open floor. Animate 'Along the route' across a shot and, with the camera looking at it, they roll through the home.

ramp.label: Entry ramp
ramp.blurb: A zero-threshold ramp at the door: a level landing, then a slope down to the ground, with handrails. The run is derived from the rise and the slope, so it is always drawn to the slope you ask for -- 1:12 is the ADA maximum.

ceiling_lift.label: Ceiling hoist
ceiling_lift.blurb: A ceiling-track patient lift slung between two points on the frame, with a carriage and a strap that lowers a sling. Because the shell is a rigid space frame, a hoist can anchor to it anywhere. Animate 'Lower the sling' for a transfer.

grab_bar.label: Grab bar
grab_bar.blurb: A wall grab bar mounted on the shell. It anchors straight to a frame member, which a stud wall can rarely promise at the exact spot a transfer needs one.

forge:ground.label: Ground pad
forge:ground.blurb: The slab the dome sits on. Mostly a visual reference so you can tell which way is down and how big the dome really is.

forge:frame.label: Strut frame
forge:frame.blurb: The load-bearing skeleton: one strut per triangle edge. A 2V dome uses exactly two strut lengths, and this layer can colour them differently so the pattern is obvious.

forge:assemblies.label: Panel assemblies
forge:assemblies.blurb: The real dome: 40 individual triangles, each with its own three struts and its own fill. Click any triangle in the 3D view to select it, then change what it is made of -- a window here, a vent there, solar on the sunny side. The three edges of one triangle do not have to use the same strut.

forge:waist_joints.label: Hourglass waist joints
forge:waist_joints.blurb: Where two equilateral triangles meet point to point, something has to make that into a real joint -- banding, wooden braces, a gusset plate, or one continuous piece. There are ten of these waists in a hemisphere.

forge:triangle_frames.label: Triangle frames (uniform)
forge:triangle_frames.blurb: How these domes are actually built: 40 separate triangular frames, each three flat-laid boards mitered at the corners, bolted to their neighbours. Every seam ends up two boards thick because each triangle brings its own -- so there are no hubs anywhere in the dome.

forge:hubs.label: Hub connectors
forge:hubs.blurb: The joints where struts meet. A 2V hemisphere has a fixed number of them, and they are where most of a real build's cost and precision goes.

forge:panels.label: Panels
forge:panels.blurb: The triangular skin between the struts. Set 'Dish depth' above zero and each panel curves inward like a golf-ball dimple, so rain runs to the middle instead of sheeting off the seams.

forge:micro_drains.label: Micro-drains
forge:micro_drains.blurb: A small outlet at the low point of each dished panel. This is what makes the dimple useful: water that pools in the dish leaves through here instead of finding a seam.

forge:veins.label: Seam veins (gasket)
forge:veins.blurb: A channel running along the inside of every seam, held clear of the outer skin by a deliberate gap. Anything that gets past a seam lands in a vein instead of dripping into the room -- which turns the classic leaky-dome complaint into plumbing.

forge:vein_water.label: Water in the veins
forge:vein_water.blurb: Animated flow inside the vein network. Every seam drains downhill toward the collector ring at the base, so you can watch where water actually goes.

forge:panel_runoff.label: Runoff on panels
forge:panel_runoff.blurb: Droplets sliding down the face of each dished panel toward its micro-drain. Only makes visual sense when Panels have some dish depth.

forge:shell.label: Shell surface
forge:shell.blurb: A continuous surface at a chosen depth -- use it as an outer rain skin, an inner liner, a vapour barrier, or a layer of insulation. Add several at different offsets to build up a real wall section.

forge:collector_ring.label: Collector ring
forge:collector_ring.blurb: The gutter around the base that every vein empties into. This is where all those separate seam channels become one flow.

forge:downpipe.label: Downpipe
forge:downpipe.blurb: The single pipe carrying collected water down into the tank.

forge:cistern.label: Cistern
forge:cistern.blurb: The tank under the dome that everything drains into. The fill level is adjustable so you can see the captured volume.

forge:rain.label: Rain
forge:rain.blurb: Falling rain above the dome, so the capture story reads at a glance. Purely visual -- it does not drive the other layers.

vo:wedge_member.label: Raw wedge member
vo:wedge_member.blurb: One eighth of a log used as a stick: pith edge in, bark face out, two flat sawn faces. The same prism the wedge films draw.

vo:timber_stick.label: Rough timber
vo:timber_stick.blurb: A stick that looks like wood: bowed, tapered, knotted, sometimes barked.

vo:board_2x4.label: Dressed two-by-four
vo:board_2x4.blurb: The store-bought board the wedge replaces, at its real 1.5 by 3.5 inch section.

vo:section_disc.label: Bucked section, end-on
vo:section_disc.blurb: A slice of trunk seen from the end, whole or split into halves, quarters or eighths, with the pieces pushed apart.

vo:wedge_shell.label: Pinwheel wedge dome
vo:wedge_shell.blurb: Forty independent pinwheel panels of raw wedges -- the dome the wedge films build.

vo:solved_dome.label: The simulator's solved dome
vo:solved_dome.blurb: The raw-wedge simulator's own finished meshes: 120 members with their compound butt cuts and, optionally, the seam keys.

vo:hub_dome.label: 2V hub dome
vo:hub_dome.blurb: The ordinary 2V hemisphere: sixty-five struts meeting at hubs.

vo:person.label: Person
vo:person.blurb: The articulated worker, posed or walking, at any height.

vo:force_arrow.label: Compression or tension
vo:force_arrow.blurb: One member with its load drawn as arrows: pointing in for compression, out for tension.

vo:dimension.label: Dimension line
vo:dimension.blurb: A measured length with end ticks and its figure above it. Pass the text as ``text``; it should come from a token, never be typed.

vo:icon.label: Pinned pictogram
vo:icon.blurb: A flat icon from two_v_demo.icons, pinned to a point in the world. Pass the icon key as ``icon``.

vo:pine_tree.label: Pine tree, standing or felled
vo:pine_tree.blurb: The book's pine: its usable trunk, taper and crown, felled with a face notch and a back cut, the chainsaw pictogram at the fell line, falling over the hinge and settling on the ground.

vo:log_sections.label: Log, bucked and split
vo:log_sections.blurb: The usable trunk on the ground, cut into the plan's sections and every section split into the plan's sectors, pushed apart into an exploded view.

vo:harvest.label: The harvest, tree to wedges
vo:harvest.blurb: The whole sequence as one object: fell, limb, buck and explode. Drive the four knobs in order across a chapter.

tree.define: A standing pine: the raw material of the whole method. The book's tree has {{tree.usable_length_ft}} feet of straight trunk, {{tree.butt_diameter_in}} inches across at the butt and {{tree.top_diameter_in}} at the top.

trunk.define: The main stem of a tree, from the stump to the branches. Only its straight lower part becomes struts.

log.define: A length of trunk once the tree is down and the branches are off.

bark.define: The rough outer skin of a tree. On a wedge it stays on the outside face, the one that ends up facing the weather.

bark face.define: The curved outer face of a wedge, still wearing its bark or the outermost growth rings. It faces out of the dome.

pith.define: The soft thread of wood at the exact centre of a trunk. Every wedge has it as its sharp inner edge, pointing into the dome.

sawn face.define: One of the two flat faces a wedge gets from the rip cuts that split it. Flat enough for the end of the next member to bear against.

grain.define: The direction the wood fibres run: along the trunk. A split follows it, which is why a split face comes out flat.

knot.define: Where a branch grew out of the trunk: a hard, dark spot that weakens the wood around it.

defect.define: Anything that spoils a length of wood for structure: a knot, a bend, a crack. Short members limit what one defect can cost.

taper.define: How a trunk narrows toward its top: here from {{tree.butt_diameter_in}} inches at the butt to {{tree.top_diameter_in}} at the top of the usable length.

stump.define: What stays in the ground after felling, with the notch and the back cut still readable on its top.

section.define: One length of trunk, bucked to {{tree.section_length_ft}} feet. A tree gives {{tree.sections}} of them, and each splits into {{tree.sectors}} struts.

sector.define: One of the equal pie-slice pieces a round section splits into: {{tree.sectors}} of them, {{tree.sector_angle_deg}} degrees each.

wedge.define: A sector of a log used as a structural member without squaring it: two flat sawn faces, a curved bark face, and the pith as a sharp edge. This book's is {{member.width_in}} inches across the bark and {{member.depth_in}} deep.

board.define: A sawn rectangle of wood: what a mill makes, and what the wedge method does without.

two-by-four.define: The commonest framing board, sold as two by four inches but dressed down to {{board.dressed_in2}} square inches of section. Its shelf price here is {{board.price_usd}} dollars.

dimensional lumber.define: Boards sawn, dried and planed to standard sizes. The whole store-bought route exists to make it.

slab.define: The rounded outer strip a sawmill cuts off each side of a log to square it. Wood lost to shape, not to quality.

cant.define: The squared middle of a log once the slabs are off. Boards are sawn from it.

offcut.define: The piece left over when a length is cut from a longer one. A deliberately long head end leaves its error in the offcut.

sawdust.define: The chips a saw throws out of its cut. In a split, the kerf's sawdust is the only wood lost.

cull.define: A board bought and then not used: bowed, twisted, wet or split. It is paid for anyway.

woodlot.define: The patch of trees a builder can actually cut from. The method sizes the dome to what grows there.

species.define: The kind of tree. The method is worked out on pine; another species changes how strong the stick is, not the arithmetic.

strut.define: A straight member of a dome frame. An ordinary 2V hub dome has {{frame.edges}}; the panelised wedge dome has {{frame.members}}, because every panel keeps its own.

member.define: Any structural piece of the frame. In the wedge dome every member is one raw wedge, and there are {{frame.members}} of them.

panel.define: One triangle of the frame, built flat on the jig and finished before it is lifted. The hemisphere has {{frame.panels}}.

hub.define: A connector where several struts meet at one point. The ordinary 2V dome needs them; the wedge dome has none.

joint.define: Where members meet. In a pinwheel panel every joint is one member's end pressed against the side of the next.

pinwheel.define: How a wedge panel's three members meet: each end butts into the side of the next, all the same way round, like the blades of a pinwheel. No end is mitred and nothing is shaved to a point.

seam.define: The line where two neighbouring panels meet. The hemisphere has {{frame.seams}}, and they close at only {{seam.distinct_angles}} different fold angles.

seam key.define: The separate strip that sits in every seam between two panels' members and takes up the angle between them, so the wood never has to be cut to it. It can be a rigid spline, a rubber hose or a gasket, {{jig.gasket_in}} inches thick here.

v-bracket.define: A strip of scrap sheet metal folded into a V and screwed into two struts. It joined the frankendome's mismatched sticks.

head overfit.define: Stock left {{jig.head_overfit_in}} inches long at a member's head end on purpose, so cutting error leaves as an offcut instead of building up around the triangle.

rim.define: The bottom edge of the dome, where panels meet the base. Its {{frame.rim_edges}} edges join nothing.

keystone.define: A panel whose opening tapers because its wedges point outward, so it cannot fall through the frame.

connector.define: Any part that joins members: a hub, a bracket, a bolt plate. The size of the connector sets how much is cut off every strut.

dome.define: A roughly spherical shell built from triangles. The book's is half a sphere of {{frame.panels}} triangles, {{dome.diameter_ft}} feet across and {{dome.height_ft}} tall at the centre.

shell.define: The dome as one closed surface: the frame plus whatever covers it. A triangulated shell carries load as a whole.

frankendome.define: The author's first dome: {{frame.panels}} triangles of mismatched sticks held by V brackets. The failure that taught the wedge method.

hemisphere.define: Half a sphere. A 2V hemisphere is the dome this project builds.

icosahedron.define: The twenty-faced regular solid every geodesic dome starts from. Its triangles are split and pushed out onto a sphere.

frequency.define: How many pieces each edge of the starting icosahedron is split into. 2V means two, which leaves just two strut lengths.

chord factor.define: The length of a strut when the sphere's radius is one. Multiply it by any real radius to get real lengths.

golden ratio.define: Phi: the number that places an icosahedron's twelve corners. It is not the ratio of a 2V dome's two strut lengths, whatever is often said.

triangle.define: The only shape that cannot change without changing a side's length, which is why every dome panel is one.

pentagon.define: A five-sided shape. Every closed cage of hexagons needs exactly twelve of them to curve round.

hexagon.define: A six-sided shape. A sheet of them lies flat forever; only pentagons let it curve.

zome.define: A dome swept from a star of directions rather than cut from a sphere. Its panels are flat rhombuses and it closes on a point.

vertex.define: A corner of the geometry, where edges meet. In the wedge dome no stick reaches one: the corners are reference points.

edge.define: A straight line between two corners of the geometry. The hemisphere has {{frame.edges}} unique edges, and the panelised frame puts two members on each interior one.

radius.define: The distance from the centre of the sphere to the shell. The book's dome has a radius of {{dome.radius_in}} inches, set by the tree.

fold angle.define: The angle between two neighbouring panels at their seam. The wedge dome's seams take only {{seam.distinct_angles}}: {{seam.fold_a_deg}} and {{seam.fold_b_deg}} degrees.

bevel.define: An angle cut along the length of a board so that two faces meet at the fold they need.

mitre.define: An angle cut across the end of a board. The pinwheel panel needs none.

cross-section.define: The shape you see when a member is cut straight across. A wedge's is a slice of pie; a board's is a rectangle.

orientation.define: Which of the four ways a wedge is turned in its panel. Each one gives the frame a different feature.

network.define: The web of members that carries load together, so no single stick has to carry it alone.

central angle.define: The angle a strut spans as seen from the sphere's centre. Every end cut follows from it.

unit sphere.define: A sphere of radius one. Working on it first turns every length into a factor that scales to any size.

projected midpoint.define: The middle of an icosahedron's edge, pushed out onto the sphere. That one move is what creates the second strut length.

board foot.define: A volume of wood: a board one foot square and one inch thick. This book's trunk holds {{tree.solid_bf}} of them.

recovery.define: The share of a trunk that ends up in usable pieces. Split into wedges this book's tree keeps {{tree.recovery_pct}} percent.

square foot.define: An area one foot by one foot, the unit floors are quoted in. The book's dome floors {{dome.floor_sqft}} of them.

strut length.define: How long a member is. The longest in the book's frame is {{dome.longest_member_in}} inches, and there are only {{dome.member_lengths}} lengths to cut.

connector deduction.define: The length taken off a strut's centre-to-centre length so its connector fits. The geometry gives hub centres; the saw needs something shorter.

tolerance.define: How far a cut or a length may be off and still work. The jig is how a builder keeps inside it forty times.

crossover.define: The trunk diameter above which one wedge is the stiffer member than a dressed two-by-four. Below it the wedge loses, and the films say so.

chainsaw.define: A hand-held saw with a toothed chain running round a bar. The whole harvest is done with one small one: {{saw.displacement_cc}} cc, a {{saw.bar_in}}-inch bar, {{saw.price_usd}} dollars.

sawmill.define: The machines that square logs into boards. The wedge method removes the whole step.

jig.define: A fixture that holds parts in the same place every time, so that forty panels come out identical. Here it is one flat bench.

table saw.define: A saw whose blade sticks up through a table, used to rip a board along its length at a set tilt.

mitre saw.define: A saw that swings to crosscut the end of a board at an angle. Its scale runs out before a hubless dome's angles do.

crosscut sled.define: A tray that slides past a table saw's blade and holds a board at a fixed angle, for cuts a mitre saw cannot reach.

stop block.define: A block clamped at a set distance, so every piece is cut to exactly the same length without measuring any of them.

truck.define: The pickup store-bought lumber rides home in. The wedge method never makes the trip.

felling.define: Bringing a standing tree down where you want it: a face notch on the side it should fall, a back cut from the other side, and the hinge between them steering it. The plan gives it {{work.felling_days}} days.

notch.define: The wedge-shaped opening cut into the side a tree is meant to fall toward.

back cut.define: The felling cut made from the far side, a little above the notch. It frees the tree and leaves the hinge.

hinge.define: The strip of uncut wood between the notch and the back cut. It holds the tree to the stump as it falls and steers it.

limbing.define: Cutting the branches off a felled tree.

bucking.define: Cutting a felled trunk into lengths: here {{tree.section_length_ft}}-foot sections, over {{work.bucking_days}} days.

splitting.define: Cutting a section lengthwise through its centre: halves, then quarters, then eighths. Nothing is squared and nothing is thrown away but the kerf.

ripping.define: Sawing along the grain. For the wedges, ripping is how a section is split, and it is the bulk of the saw work: {{work.ripping_hours}} hours for a whole frame.

kerf.define: The width of wood a saw cut turns into sawdust. A chain's kerf is {{saw.kerf_in}} inches, and across a trunk it costs {{tree.kerf_bf}} board feet: the only wood a split loses.

milling.define: Turning a log into boards: slabbing, squaring, resawing, edging, trimming, drying and planing. From tree to graded board it takes {{route.mill_steps}} operations.

crosscut.define: A cut straight across the grain.

drying.define: Letting green wood lose water, so it shrinks before it is in the frame rather than after.

butt cut.define: The one compound-angle cut on each wedge, made at the end that presses into its neighbour, with the member held in a cradle.

flush-cut.define: Cutting a member's deliberately long head off level with its neighbour, in place on the jig, so the panel comes out true without measuring.

end cut.define: The angled cut at a strut's end where it meets a hub. Its angle is half the strut's central angle.

raising.define: Lifting the finished panels into place, bottom ring first. The plan's last two days.

harvest.define: Everything the chainsaw does, from the first felling cut to the last strut stacked: {{work.harvest_days}} days in the plan.

cut list.define: The list of every length to cut and how many of each: the step from a drawing to a pile of sticks.

compression.define: Being pushed on along a member's length. A triangulated shell loads its members mostly this way or in tension, not in bending.

tension.define: Being pulled along a member's length.

bending.define: Being loaded across a member's length, like a plank bridging a gap. It is where a wedge is weakest: {{versus.strength_pct}} percent against a dressed two-by-four from a {{versus.diameter_in}}-inch log.

load.define: The weight and push a structure has to carry: its own weight, snow, wind and people.

racking.define: A rectangle folding into a parallelogram under a sideways push. A triangle cannot rack.

stiffness.define: How much a member resists bending. It grows fast with a section's depth, which is why a wedge turned the right way does well.

shelf price.define: What a board costs on the store rack: {{board.price_usd}} dollars for the two-by-four compared here. Very little of it is the tree.

middleman.define: Anyone who handles a board between the tree and the rack and takes a share of its price. The why film lists every one.

overhead.define: Costs that ride along with a purchase without being on the receipt: trips, culls, time spent waiting.

rate.define: How fast the work goes, or what an hour of it is worth. Measured by what it replaces, an hour of cutting is worth {{work.rate_dressed_usd}} dollars against dressed two-by-fours.

bom.define: The full list of parts to buy, with quantities and prices.

floor area.define: How much floor the dome gives: {{dome.floor_sqft}} square feet for the book's dome, sized by the tree rather than chosen.

riser wall.define: A short upright wall under the dome that buys headroom near the edge.

base ring.define: The bottom ring where the lowest panels land. An error in it is carried all the way round.

foundation.define: What the dome stands on. Whichever kind it is, it has to be level and it has to hold the ring.

opening.define: A doorway or window. In a dome, take out whole panels rather than cutting members.

skin.define: What covers the frame against weather: sheathing, membrane, cladding. A frame is not a shelter until it has one.

utility core.define: One straight column carrying plumbing and power, so a round room's curves never have to meet a pipe.

plenum.define: A duct ring round the base that lets one blower move air through the whole dome.

solar panel.define: A panel that turns sunlight into electricity. The model puts them only on dome faces that actually face the sun.

fuel.define: What the saw burns. Ripping the whole frame takes {{fuel.rip_tanks}} tanks: between {{fuel.rip_gallons}} and {{fuel.rip_gallons_high}} US gallons, a range because the saw's tank size is not confirmed.

bar oil.define: Oil the saw drips onto its chain as it cuts, counted alongside the fuel in the timed sessions.

sheet metal.define: Thin flat metal. The frankendome's V brackets were cut from a washing machine's casing.

builder.define: Whoever cuts, assembles and raises the dome. In this story, one person with a saw and occasional help.

engineer.define: The professional who sizes members and signs off a structure meant to be lived in. The films say where one is needed.

fortnight.define: The book's build window: {{work.days}} days from the saw to a standing frame, {{work.harvest_days}} of them spent harvesting.

session.define: One sitting of cutting, timed, with the output and the fuel written down. The whole cost argument rests on two of them.

token.define: A named figure written into a script in double braces and filled in from the code on every build, so the words and the arithmetic cannot drift apart.

callout.define: A figure on screen that arrives with the words that say it: a value, a unit, a pictogram and a short note, held long enough to read.

tally.define: A column of figures that builds an arithmetic chain a row at a time, and is checked so it cannot show a sum that does not work out.

beat.define: One chapter, or a claim with the screen that proves it, rendered to its own file so that fixing it costs one short render.

chapter.define: One step of a film: a headline, the narration, the figures on screen, and the picture that goes with them.

visual object.define: A drawable noun with named knobs -- a tree with a felling knob, a log with an exploded-view knob -- that any film or presentation can place and animate by moving one number.

painter.define: The function that draws one kind of picture as a pure function of how far through its chapter the film is. The same moment always gives the same frame.

camera.define: The viewpoint the frame is drawn from: where it is, what it looks at, and how wide it sees.

pixel.define: One dot of the picture. Everything the films compute ends as a colour for each of them.

data.numbers: every on-screen number is computed by code that proves it; borrowed values are named external constants with unit + source, printed in the report
data.determinism: seed every random generator; frames are pure functions of (stage, progress)
data.reuse: reuse segments/figure/timber/visual_objects/lexicon and the bridges before drawing anything new
data.stills_first: render one still per chapter/scene and look at every one before exporting
data.verify: verify by frame count (nb_frames ~ duration*fps), not by duration alone
data.append_only: rendered output is append-only; re-renders land beside the old cut as -v2/-v3
data.corrections: corrections are chapters on camera, not silent re-cuts
data.sequential: never run voiced exports in parallel (speech endpoint throttles)
data.camera_traps: lay rows along X (+X is screen left at yaw 90); distance ~2x object size; keep the left third clear in teaching style; nothing straddles z=0
